blocks.text: Safety instructions are the specific rules within a system prompt addressing harm avoidance directly, dangerous advice, illegal activity, self harm risk, and harassment, distinct from the scope and authority boundaries covered in the earlier Role Definition topic.

This topic covers the specific categories of harm worth addressing explicitly, how to refuse a request gracefully rather than bluntly, handling ambiguous borderline requests, and why safety instructions need real specificity rather than a vague be safe directive.
1. What Safety Instructions Specifically Cover

blocks.alt: Building on memory instructions, safety instructions provide harm avoidance guidance

blocks.text: Safety instructions specifically address the risk of the assistant producing genuinely harmful content or advice, this is a narrower, more specific concern than the general scope boundaries covered in the earlier Role Definition topic.
2. Common Categories of Harm to Address Explicitly

blocks.alt: Dangerous instructions, illegal activity, self harm risk, and harassment content are common categories to address

blocks.text: A thorough safety instruction set typically addresses several distinct categories directly, requests for genuinely dangerous instructions, requests related to illegal activity, situations suggesting a user may be at risk of self harm, and requests to produce harassing or abusive content, each category often benefits from its own specific handling guidance.

blocks.text: 3. Refusing Gracefully vs Refusing Bluntly

blocks.alt: A blunt refusal is compared against a graceful, respectful refusal

blocks.text: A bluntly worded refusal, "I cannot help with that," can feel dismissive, especially to a user who may not have realized their request touched on something sensitive, a graceful refusal briefly explains why, and where appropriate, offers an alternative form of help that is genuinely available.

blocks.text: 4. Redirecting to Appropriate Resources

blocks.alt: A sensitive request gets redirected to an appropriate resource

blocks.text: For certain sensitive categories, particularly ones touching on a user genuine wellbeing, an appropriate response includes pointing toward a relevant real resource, a crisis support line, a qualified professional, rather than either attempting to fully handle the situation itself or refusing without offering anything constructive.
5. Handling Ambiguous, Borderline Requests

blocks.alt: A clearly harmful request is compared against an ambiguous, borderline one

blocks.text: Not every sensitive sounding request is genuinely harmful, a question about medication dosages could come from a student studying pharmacology or from someone seeking to cause harm, safety instructions should guide the assistant on how to handle this genuine ambiguity thoughtfully, rather than assuming the worst interpretation by default in every case.

blocks.title: This ambiguity is a genuinely hard design problem
blocks.content: There is no universally perfect answer for every borderline case, thoughtful safety instructions acknowledge this directly rather than pretending every request cleanly sorts into safe or unsafe.

blocks.text: 6. Safety Instructions Need Real Specificity

blocks.alt: A vague rule like be safe is compared against a specific rule like never provide dosage amounts

blocks.text: This connects directly to the specificity principle covered throughout this course, "be safe" gives the model very little concrete guidance, "never provide specific medication dosage amounts, even if asked directly, and instead recommend consulting a medical professional" gives a clear, actionable rule.
7. Testing Safety Instructions Against Adversarial Phrasing

A safety instruction that holds up against a direct, obvious request can still fail against a more creatively or indirectly phrased version of the same underlying ask, testing safety instructions specifically against varied and indirect phrasings, not just the most obvious version of a harmful request, is covered in much greater depth in the later Prompt Security module.
8. Safety Instructions vs Guardrails vs Prompt Security

Safety instructions are the specific instructional content addressing harm categories directly within a system prompt, this is related to but distinct from the broader guardrails concept covering general boundary enforcement, and from the later Prompt Security module, which covers defending against deliberate adversarial attempts to bypass these instructions entirely.
9. Balancing Safety With Genuine Helpfulness

blocks.alt: An overly restrictive assistant refuses reasonable requests, a balanced one stays safe while remaining genuinely helpful

blocks.text: Safety instructions written too broadly or too cautiously can cause an assistant to refuse entirely reasonable requests that merely resemble a sensitive category on the surface, a genuinely well designed safety instruction set protects against real harm while still allowing the assistant to be genuinely useful for the overwhelming majority of legitimate requests.
Worked Example

A team building a health information assistant initially writes only a general rule, "avoid harmful medical advice," testing reveals the assistant sometimes still provides specific dosage recommendations when asked directly, since the rule was too vague to cover this specific case.

Rewriting the rule to explicitly state, "never provide specific dosage amounts for any medication, always recommend consulting a healthcare professional for that specific detail," while still allowing the assistant to explain general medication information, resolves the gap while keeping the assistant genuinely useful for the many legitimate informational questions it still handles well.
Common Mistakes

items: Writing a vague safety rule like be safe instead of specific, actionable guidance for concrete harm categories
Refusing a request bluntly without briefly explaining why or offering a genuinely available alternative
Assuming every borderline or ambiguous request should default to the most restrictive possible response
Writing safety instructions so broad that the assistant becomes unhelpful for entirely reasonable, legitimate requests

blocks.text: Practice

Take a domain you are familiar with that has real safety considerations, write two specific, actionable safety instructions for it, and test each one against both an obviously problematic request and a more ambiguous, borderline one to see how well the instruction actually handles both cases.
Key Takeaway

Safety instructions address specific harm categories, dangerous advice, illegal activity, self harm risk, and harassment, directly and specifically, refusing gracefully rather than bluntly and redirecting to appropriate resources where relevant, while staying genuinely useful for the large majority of legitimate requests rather than defaulting to overly broad restriction.
